newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU tensions overshadow Franco-German summit.
newsitem.headline: EMU tensions overshadow Franco-German summit.

text.p: Franco-German tensions over the European Union's single currency were on full display on Monday as President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl met to launch an initiative for this week's EU summit in Dublin.

Even before the two leaders met in Nuremberg, in southern Germany, senior officials from Paris and Bonn were making statements defending their divergent views on how to set up a "stability pact" to defend the planned currency, the euro.

Chirac and Kohl, whose alliance is the motor of the EU's integration drive, were all smiles as they briefly visited the glittering Christmas Market in the mediaeval city before starting their regular six-monthly summit.

Their day-long talks were due to focus on strains over Bonn's demand for a strict "stability pact" for the euro, a joint letter on EU reforms the leaders want to send before Friday's summit and a bid to save money on joint defence programmes.
"What we need is a solid currency that gives us the strength to create tomorrow's jobs," French Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said before the opening ceremony.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe fired a shot across Germany's bow on Monday morning with a Financial Times interview calling for elected politicians to have some influence over the future European Central Bank (ECB).

"We don't want all decisions on economic, budgetary, fiscal and monetary policy to be shaped by a technocratic, automatic system under the sole authority of the ECB," he said. "That is not our concept of democracy."
Germany, whose concept of democracy includes shielding monetary stability from what it sees as potential abuse by politicians, promptly fired back.
"Germany is very clear on this point," said Werner Hoyer, the foreign ministry state secretary for European affairs.
"The independence of the European Central Bank is one of the great achievements of the Maastricht Treaty and is not up for discussion," he told German Radio on Monday morning.
The dispute goes to the heart of how the future economic and monetary union (EMU) is supposed to work.

Germany, which will give up Europe's hardest currency when it joins the planned EMU in 1999, says member states must agree to maintain strict budgetary discipline and accept almost iron-clad automatic fines if they overspend.
France, with its long tradition of state intervention, speaks for a majority of EU states looking for more flexibility for EMU members which temporarily stray from this strict path.

Bonn's hard negotiating on the stability pact has sparked protests from French politicians and talk of a "German diktat". French former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing has suggested a depreciation of the franc before France joins EMU.

"This is a clash of different philosophies and cultures, based on the very different paths we have taken in Europe," Hoyer said, adding that the independent European Central Bank was a big concession to Germany by other EU states in Maastricht.
The lively debate over EMU in Paris showed "how much pressure we're under, especially in France," he said.

In a clear hint to Bonn that it would have to give ground, Juppe said in his interview: "I think France is the key. If France is not ready in time (to enter EMU in 1999) there will be no EMU for a long period."
He said the political leaders of member states should meet "periodically to fix broad lines of economic policy, dialogue with the central bank and give their opinion".

One element of this "political power" would be to influence exchange rate policy -- exactly the kind of idea Germans see leading to the inflation they traditionally fear. The French aim is to ensure the euro is not overvalued against the dollar, making European exports less competitive.
